title: Universal distress signals
summary: Get spotted when you cannot call.
steps: Rule of 3: three whistle blasts, three fires in a triangle, three flashes of light, repeated regularly.
SOS in Morse: 3 short, 3 long, 3 short (· · · — — — · · ·) with a light or a whistle.
Ground-to-air signals visible from aircraft: a large V = need help, a large X = need medical assistance. Letters several metres high, contrasting with the ground.
In daytime: a mirror or a phone screen to reflect the sun towards an aircraft or a ridge.
Stay near an open, visible area.
tips: A whistle carries much further than your voice and doesn't tire you: attach one to every bag.

title: Walkie-talkies, CB and FM radio
summary: Stay informed and in touch with your family without a mobile network.
steps: Battery or hand-crank FM/AM radio: to hear official instructions (in France, France Bleu / ICI and France Inter are the designated crisis stations; elsewhere, your national public broadcaster).
PMR446 walkie-talkies: licence-free in Europe (FRS in North America), range from a few hundred metres in town to a few kilometres in open country. Agree on a channel and listening times in advance.
CB (27 MHz): channel 19 is used by truck drivers, channel 9 is traditionally reserved for emergencies.
Amateur radio: emergency networks exist, but transmitting requires a licence (except in genuine distress).
tips: Set a radio appointment: for example 5 minutes at the top of every hour, to save batteries.

title: Family communication plan
summary: Agree BEFOREHAND, because you may not be able to call each other afterwards.
steps: Choose two meeting points: one near home, one outside the neighbourhood.
Name a relay contact far away whom everyone will notify.
Write down important numbers on paper (nobody knows them by heart any more) and keep them in every bag.
Agree on a walkie-talkie channel and listening times.
Leave a written message on site (door, letterbox) saying where you have gone.

title: Messaging without Internet (Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, LoRa)
summary: Apps and devices can pass messages from one phone to the next.
steps: Install BEFORE the crisis a mesh messaging app that works over Bluetooth/Wi-Fi Direct (e.g. Briar, Bridgefy).
Set it up and test it with your family while everything still works.
Range: a few dozen metres per device, messages hop from one phone to another.
For more range: small LoRa radios (e.g. Meshtastic) relay text messages over several kilometres without a network.
warnings: These solutions must be installed and tested while the Internet is working.

title: The Morse alphabet
summary: Send a message with a light, a whistle or knocks.
steps: Dot = short signal; dash = long signal (3 times a dot).
Leave a short silence between the signals of a letter, a longer one (3 dots) between letters, and longer still (7 dots) between words.
Most useful letters: S = · · ·  O = — — —  E = ·  T = —  A = · —  N = — ·  I = · ·  M = — —.
SOS: · · · — — — · · · as a single block, then a pause, and start again.
Use the app's Morse tool to translate and send any message automatically, or to listen to and decode one.

title: The radio alphabet (spelling without mistakes)
summary: To spell a name or address over radio or phone in a noisy place.
steps: A Alfa, B Bravo, C Charlie, D Delta, E Echo, F Foxtrot, G Golf, H Hotel, I India.
J Juliett, K Kilo, L Lima, M Mike, N November, O Oscar, P Papa, Q Quebec, R Romeo.
S Sierra, T Tango, U Uniform, V Victor, W Whiskey, X X-ray, Y Yankee, Z Zulu.
Numbers: say them one digit at a time (“one - two - five” for 125).
End of message: “Over”; to end the conversation: “Over and out” (strictly, “Out”).

title: Organising neighbourhood mutual aid
summary: Without the Internet, information travels through neighbours.
steps: Identify in advance the vulnerable people in the building or street (elderly, sick, living alone).
Set a daily meeting point and time to share news.
Use a notice board (hallway, town hall): needs, offers, official information.
Pool resources: radio, tools, solar chargers, skills (nurse, electrician).
Always check information with an official source (radio) before passing it on.
